question_text: Which of the following inclusion relations is always correct?
explanation: Every natural number is an integer, so N ⊆ Z. Integers need not be natural, rational numbers need not be integers, and real numbers need not be rational.

question_text: Let A be the set of all multiples of 6 and B be the set of all multiples of 3. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 3, since 6k = 3(2k). Hence A ⊆ B.

question_text: If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C, which of the following inclusion relations must be correct?
explanation: Subset relation is transitive: if every element of A is in B and every element of B is in C, then every element of A is in C. Thus A ⊆ C.

question_text: Let S = {n² : n ∈ Z} and T be the set of all non-negative integers. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: The square of every integer is a non-negative integer, so S ⊆ T. But not every non-negative integer is a perfect square.

question_text: For real intervals, which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every number strictly between 1 and 2 also lies in the closed interval [1, 2]. Hence (1, 2) ⊆ [1, 2].

question_text: Let A = {x ∈ Z : x is divisible by 10} and B = {x ∈ Z : x is even}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: If x is divisible by 10, then x = 10k = 2(5k), so x is even. Therefore A ⊆ B.

question_text: Let P be the set of all prime numbers greater than 2 and O be the set of all odd positive integers. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every prime number greater than 2 is odd. Therefore P ⊆ O, while many odd positive integers such as 9 are not prime.

question_text: Let A = {x ∈ R : 0 < x < 1} and B = {x ∈ R : 0 ≤ x ≤ 1}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every real number satisfying 0 < x < 1 also satisfies 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Hence A ⊆ B.

question_text: If A ⊆ B, which inclusion relation involving an arbitrary set C is always correct?
explanation: If x ∈ A ∩ C, then x ∈ A and x ∈ C. Since A ⊆ B, x ∈ B also. Therefore x ∈ B ∩ C, so A ∩ C ⊆ B ∩ C.

question_text: If X ⊆ Y, which of the following inclusion relations is always correct for any set Z?
explanation: If an element belongs to X \ Z, it belongs to X and not to Z. Since X ⊆ Y, it also belongs to Y and not to Z. Hence X \ Z ⊆ Y \ Z.

question_text: Let A = {x ∈ Z : 12 divides x} and B = {x ∈ Z : 4 divides x}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every multiple of 12 is also a multiple of 4 because 12k = 4(3k). Thus A ⊆ B.

question_text: Let A be the solution set of x² - 5x + 6 = 0 and B be the solution set of (x - 2)(x - 3)(x - 4) = 0. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: A = {2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}. Hence every element of A is in B, so A ⊆ B.

question_text: Let D be the set of all differentiable real-valued functions on R and C be the set of all continuous real-valued functions on R. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every differentiable function is continuous, but not every continuous function is differentiable. Therefore D ⊆ C.

question_text: Let A be the set of all 2 × 2 matrices having one complete row equal to zero, and let B be the set of all singular 2 × 2 matrices. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: A matrix with a complete zero row has determinant 0, so it is singular. Hence A ⊆ B.

question_text: Let E be the set of all equilateral triangles and I be the set of all isosceles triangles, where an isosceles triangle means a triangle with at least two equal sides. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so it certainly has at least two equal sides. Therefore E ⊆ I.

question_text: Let A = {x ∈ R : |x - 1| < 2} and B = {x ∈ R : -2 < x < 4}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: |x - 1| < 2 gives -1 < x < 3. Since every x in (-1, 3) also lies in (-2, 4), A ⊆ B.

question_text: Let T be the set of all real numbers with terminating decimal expansion and Q be the set of rational numbers. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every terminating decimal can be written as an integer divided by a power of 10, so it is rational. Hence T ⊆ Q.

question_text: If A ⊆ B, which inclusion relation between their power sets is always correct?
explanation: Every subset of A is also a subset of B when A ⊆ B. Therefore every element of P(A) lies in P(B), so P(A) ⊆ P(B).

question_text: In R², let D = {(x, y) : x² + y² ≤ 1} and S = {(x, y) : |x| ≤ 1 and |y| ≤ 1}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: If (x, y) ∈ D, then x² ≤ 1 and y² ≤ 1, so |x| ≤ 1 and |y| ≤ 1. Hence D ⊆ S. The reverse is false because (1, 1) ∈ S but not in D.

question_text: Let V be the set of all real polynomials of degree at most 3. Define S = {p ∈ V : p(0) = 0 and p'(0) = 0} and T = {p ∈ V : p(0) = 0}. Which inclusion relation is correct?
explanation: Every polynomial in S satisfies p(0) = 0 as part of its defining conditions, so it belongs to T. Therefore S ⊆ T.
